description: I'm an independent citizen scientist from Ecuador with experience analyzing NASA TESS data, exoplanet candidates, and false positives. For Space Apps 2026, I'm exploring a SPHEREx project that makes scientific discovery accessible to everyone. I use AI-assisted programming and seek teammates skilled in Python, web development, astronomy, or UI/UX design.
summary:
SkyClues — Explore the Invisible. Discover What Moves.

SkyClues is an interactive web application that makes NASA's SPHEREx infrared observations accessible to everyone. Users can search by object name or sky coordinates, explore an astronomical atlas, and compare real SPHEREx images from different dates. Its Time Explorer provides animations and image blinking, while Spectrum Explorer generates infrared spectra on demand.

SkyClues addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by making changes in the sky easier to detect and understand. Beyond visual comparisons, it analyzes astronomical images to measure the movement of stars, asteroids, and comets. Tests using authentic SPHEREx observations have produced motion measurements for the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS and other Solar System objects, including uncertainties and reference-star checks.

Astronomical archives contain extraordinary scientific information, but accessing and interpreting it often requires specialized expertise. SkyClues bridges this gap, empowering students, educators, and citizen scientists to explore real observations, understand astronomical phenomena, and participate in the search for discoveries.

Our mission is to transform infrared data into an accessible window for scientific exploration.
details:
SkyClues — Project Details

What does SkyClues do?

SkyClues is an interactive astronomical exploration platform designed to make NASA's SPHEREx infrared observations accessible to students, educators, citizen scientists, and the general public.

The application brings together two complementary scientific tools: Time Explorer, for investigating changes in the sky, and Spectrum Explorer, for exploring the infrared information recorded by SPHEREx.

Users can search for astronomical objects by name, enter Right Ascension and Declination coordinates, or select a region through an interactive sky atlas. They can adjust the field of view and explore observations without requiring specialized astronomical software.

How does it work?

Time Explorer retrieves authentic SPHEREx observations from different dates and displays them as interactive sequences. Users can play animations, blink between exposures, and examine changes in the positions of astronomical objects.

Beyond visual comparison, SkyClues incorporates motion-analysis algorithms that measure apparent displacement relative to reference stars. The application can report measured motion, angular velocity, uncertainties, and the evidence supporting its conclusions.

For known Solar System and interstellar objects, SkyClues integrates NASA/IPAC's Moving Object Search Tool (MOST) to identify observations along their predicted trajectories. This enables the analysis of asteroids and comets that move between different regions of the sky.

A key demonstration is the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS. Using authentic SPHEREx observations, SkyClues measured its apparent displacement at approximately 166 ± 3 arcseconds over 99 minutes, using 16 reference stars. This demonstrates how the platform can move beyond image visualization to quantitative scientific analysis.

Spectrum Explorer takes advantage of SPHEREx's 102 nominal infrared spectral channels. Users can examine images at different wavelengths, create false-color combinations, and extract exploratory infrared spectra from selected sky positions.

The two explorers provide complementary ways to investigate the same universe: how astronomical objects change over time and how their infrared properties vary with wavelength.

SkyClues also combines compatible infrared exposures to improve signal visibility and provides an exploratory spectral interpreter that compares measured features with documented physical references, while explicitly communicating uncertainty and alternative explanations.

What makes SkyClues creative?

SkyClues combines astronomical visualization, object discovery tools, temporal analysis, and infrared spectroscopy in a unified, accessible experience.

Rather than simply displaying astronomical images, it helps users investigate the evidence behind what they observe.

Its motion-analysis capabilities distinguish predicted object positions from measured detections, use background stars as references, and account for observational limitations.

The interface also supports different levels of explanation, allowing beginners to understand results while giving experienced users access to more detailed scientific information.

Technologies and development

SkyClues was developed primarily using Python, Streamlit, JavaScript, and astronomical data-processing tools, including Astropy.

It integrates Aladin Lite for interactive sky visualization, astronomical catalogs such as Gaia and WISE, and NASA/IPAC-IRSA services for accessing authentic SPHEREx observations.

The project processes astronomical FITS data, spatial coordinates, observation metadata, and quality flags. Its scientific algorithms are tested using synthetic cases and real astronomical observations.

Development has been supported by AI coding assistants, including Claude Code and Codex, with human-directed scientific objectives, implementation decisions, testing, and evaluation.

What impact do we hope to achieve?

Modern astronomical missions produce enormous amounts of scientific data, but accessing and interpreting these observations often requires specialized knowledge.

SkyClues aims to reduce that barrier.

By providing an intuitive environment for exploring real infrared observations, the platform can support astronomy education, citizen science, and independent scientific investigation.

Our goal is to help people move beyond simply looking at astronomical images toward understanding and investigating the physical evidence they contain.

SkyClues is designed to make the infrared universe not only visible, but explorable.
